v16.title: Signals arrive
v16.intro: Angular 16 introduced signals as a reactive primitive, plus DestroyRef, required inputs and router input binding. Each card below is live: use it, then compare the code before and now.

cart.title: signal · computed · effect
cart.description: Accessory cart: quantities are a signal, totals are computed, and an effect reacts to every change.

search.title: toSignal + debounceTime + switchMap
search.description: Type to search vehicles. RxJS debounces and cancels stale requests; the result is read as a signal.
search.label: Search brand or model
search.hint: Start typing — requests wait 300 ms after your last keystroke.

destroy.title: DestroyRef · takeUntilDestroyed
destroy.description: A live telemetry feed subscribes to an interval. Unmount it and the subscription is cleaned up automatically.
destroy.unmounted: Telemetry unmounted — no subscription left behind.

required.title: Required inputs with transform
required.description: The price tag requires an amount and power; transforms turn HTML attribute strings into numbers and booleans.
required.dynamic: Bound to controls (strings in, numbers out):

binding.title: withComponentInputBinding
binding.description: The ?vehicle= query parameter is bound straight into a component input by the router. Click a link and watch the URL.
binding.hint: Pick a vehicle above — the last link triggers a 404 Problem Details.

v17.title: Control flow & defer
v17.intro: Angular 17 brought built-in control flow (@if, @for, @switch), deferrable views and — in 17.1/17.2 — signal inputs, model() and signal queries.

for.title: @for with track and @empty
for.description: Up to {{rows}} stock units. Generate them, switch the tracking strategy, then refresh or shuffle and watch how many table rows the browser had to create.
for.filter: Filter by model, dealer or VIN
for.notLoaded: No stock loaded yet — generate the units to start (@empty).

defer.title: @defer (on viewport)
defer.description: The chart below lives in its own lazy chunk. It is only downloaded when you scroll it into view.
defer.placeholder: @placeholder — the chart chunk has not been requested yet.

io.title: input() · model() · output()
io.description: Each rating is a child component: label is a required input, the value is a two-way model() and every pick emits an output().
io.reset: Set both to 1 from the parent

queries.title: viewChild · viewChildren (signal queries)
queries.description: Pre-delivery checklist. The parent queries its children as signals, so the progress is a plain computed.

vt.title: withViewTransitions
vt.description: Switching the layout is a router navigation (?layout=). The browser animates every car to its new position with the View Transitions API.

v18.title: Zoneless preview
v18.intro: Angular 18 shipped experimental zoneless change detection, @let (18.1), ng-content fallbacks, unified form events and functional redirects. This app itself runs without zone.js.

zoneless.title: Zoneless change detection
zoneless.description: No zone.js here. Each button changes a value inside setTimeout. Only the signal tells Angular to re-render; the plain field stays stale until something else schedules a check.
zoneless.explain: With zone.js, both timers would trigger a check of the whole app. Zoneless, the click itself schedules one check (counter +1), but the plain-field timer does not — press markForCheck() to reveal its real value.

let.title: @let — template variables
let.description: Leasing calculator: net amount, monthly rate and total are declared once with @let and reused in the template.

fallback.title: ng-content fallback
fallback.description: Both cards are the same component. The first projects nothing into its title slot, so the fallback content renders.
fallback.defaultBody: No [card-title] projected — the <h2> inside <ng-content> is used.
fallback.customBody: A [card-title] element was projected, so the fallback is skipped.

events.title: control.events — unified form events
events.description: Every change in this Reactive Form arrives through one stream: value, status, touched, pristine, submit and reset.
events.vinHint: 17 characters, no I, O or Q

redirect.title: redirectTo as a function
redirect.description: Old deep links like /v18/legacy/golf-7 are redirected by a function that keeps the model as a query param.
redirect.result: Redirected from legacy link "{{model}}" by a functional redirectTo.
redirect.hint: Click a legacy link to see the redirect.

v19.title: linkedSignal & resource
v19.intro: Angular 19 added linkedSignal for writable derived state and the resource APIs for async data as signals. @let became stable.

linked.title: linkedSignal — country → city
linked.description: The city is derived from the country but stays writable: pick any city, then switch country and it resets to the first city of the new list.

resource.title: resource() — dealers in the selected city
resource.description: A Promise-based loader with fetch() and an AbortSignal. Change the city quickly: the previous request is aborted, and the old list stays visible (dimmed) while reloading.

rx.title: rxResource() — vehicles by fuel type
rx.description: The same idea with an Observable stream through HttpClient, so all four interceptors (base URL, loading bar, Problem Details, mock backend) apply.
rx.failed: The vehicle service returned 503 Service unavailable.

v20.title: Stable signals
v20.intro: Angular 20 promoted effect, linkedSignal, toSignal and zoneless (20.2) to stable, and widened template expressions. httpResource, introduced in 19.2, is stable in v22.

stability.title: From developer preview to stable
stability.description: Every API used in this lab, from the version it appeared in to the version it became stable.
stability.caption: API stability per Angular version
stability.source: Stable versions come from the @publicApi tags in the installed @angular 22.2.3 typings.

http.title: httpResource — loading, error, empty, reload
http.description: One declaration covers all four states. Pick a scenario: the mock backend answers through the real interceptor chain.
http.empty: No vehicles in stock right now.

expr.title: New template expressions
expr.description: Template literals, the exponentiation operator, the in operator and void — written directly in the template, without helper methods.

v21.title: Signal Forms & Aria
v21.intro: Angular 21 made zoneless the default, introduced experimental Signal Forms and the headless Angular Aria package, and added automatic cleanup of route injectors.

forms.title: Signal Forms — contact a dealer
forms.description: The model is a plain signal; form() adds validation and field state as signals. Edit a field and watch the model and state update live.
forms.name: Full name
forms.sent: Thanks, {{name}} — a dealer will contact you.

aria.title: Angular Aria — accessible headless widgets
aria.description: Tabs, a listbox and a menu from this lab's design system. Angular Aria provides roles, focus management and keyboard support; the styles are ours.

panels.overview: Volkswagen ID.7 Tourer — the electric estate for long distances.

cleanup.title: Automatic cleanup of route injectors
cleanup.description: Each service bay is a route with its own providers. Switch bays: the route's EnvironmentInjector is destroyed and its service runs ngOnDestroy.
cleanup.none: No route injector created yet — open a bay.

v22.title: OnPush by default
v22.intro: Angular 22 makes OnPush the default strategy (Default is renamed Eager), stabilises Signal Forms and the Resource API, and adds @Service, injectAsync, debounced and exhaustive @switch.

cd.title: OnPush by default vs Eager
cd.description: Both children receive the same input. Change state that only the parent reads, then change the input, and compare the counters.
cd.explain: The parent re-renders on every click. Only the Eager child is checked along with it; the OnPush child is checked only when its input changes.

forms.title: Test-drive booking — Reactive Forms vs Signal Forms
forms.description: The same form, built twice. Submit with an address ending in @blocked.test to see how each API maps a 422 Problem Details error onto the e-mail field.

lazy.title: @Service() + injectAsync() with prefetch
lazy.description: The CSV export service sits in its own chunk. It is prefetched when the browser is idle; the click awaits it — usually instantly.

active.explain: Navigate with the sidenav and the values update — they are plain signals derived from router state.

lifecycle.title: Lifecycle & change detection
lifecycle.intro: What runs when a component is created, updated and destroyed — measured live in this app, not copied from the docs. Every log on this page comes from real hooks running in Angular 22, zoneless and OnPush by default.

hooks.title: Component lifecycle, live
hooks.description: The child implements all eight classic hooks and registers the modern APIs (effect, afterNextRender, afterRenderEffect, DestroyRef). Each button is one user action; the log lists every call it caused, in order.
hooks.t1: Creation order: constructor (field initializers, inject()) → ngOnChanges → ngOnInit → ngDoCheck → effect() → content hooks → view hooks → afterNextRender / afterRenderEffect once the DOM is up to date.
hooks.t2: ngOnChanges runs only when an input changes. A parent-only change still runs ngDoCheck and both *Checked hooks, even though the OnPush child is not re-rendered — keep them cheap or avoid them.
hooks.t3: Required inputs are not available in the constructor (NG0950): read them in computed(), effect() or ngOnInit, never in a field initializer.
hooks.t4: On destroy, ngOnDestroy runs first and then the DestroyRef callbacks — the mechanism takeUntilDestroyed() and toSignal() use to clean up.

modern.title: Classic hooks → modern APIs
modern.description: Signals remove most reasons to implement a hook. This is the mapping to apply when migrating a component.

rows.constructor: inject() works in field initializers and the constructor (the injection context). Inputs are not set yet.
rows.onChanges: Derived state is a computed(). A value that resets when an input changes but stays writable is a linkedSignal().
rows.onInit: Still fine for one-off imperative work that needs inputs. Loading data usually becomes a resource() / httpResource() keyed on the inputs.
rows.doCheck: Custom dirty checking is exactly what signals replace. Keep it only to integrate mutable third-party objects.
rows.content: Query results are signals: derive from them with computed() instead of waiting for a hook.
rows.viewInit: viewChild() is a signal, undefined until the view exists. afterNextRender() is for one-time DOM work: focus, measuring, third-party widgets.
rows.viewChecked: Runs after a render only when the signals it read changed, split into read/write phases — instead of after every check.
rows.onDestroy: Register cleanup next to the code that needs it. Works in services and plain functions too, not only components.

phases.earlyRead: read the DOM before anything is written (measure layout)
phases.write: write to the DOM; never read here
phases.mixed: read and write; the default for a single callback, avoid it when you can
phases.read: read the DOM after all writes

modern.phasesExplain: Angular runs each phase for every component before moving to the next one, so reads and writes are batched and the browser computes layout once. Each phase receives the previous phase's value as a signal. Render hooks never run on the server.

tree.title: Change detection tree
tree.description: Six components, two strategies. Each number counts how many times that component's view was refreshed. Send a notification and see which views Angular actually touches.
tree.hint: Also try the button inside Leaf A2.

actions.signal: Set a signal read only by A1

why.signal: A signal read in a template marks only that view for refresh. Its ancestors are traversed to reach it but not re-rendered, even the OnPush ones.
why.input: The root reads plate(), so it refreshes. Branch B is Eager and refreshes with its parent; Leaf B1 is OnPush but got a new input. Branch A (OnPush, nothing changed) is skipped — and so is the Eager Leaf A2 inside it.
why.plain: No signal, no event in the tree, no markForCheck(): without zone.js nobody tells Angular that something changed. A1 keeps the old value until something else refreshes it.
why.event: A template event marks its view and all its ancestors dirty, like markForCheck(). Root, Branch A and A2 refresh; Eager Branch B refreshes because its parent did. The OnPush leaves A1 and B1 are skipped.

tree.t1: Zoneless Angular schedules change detection only on notifications: a signal read by a template changes, a template event fires, an input changes, markForCheck() is called, or the async pipe receives a value.
tree.t2: OnPush (the v22 default) skips a component unless it is notified or receives a new input reference. Eager (formerly Default) is checked whenever its parent is.
tree.t3: Signals are the finest grain: only the views that read the signal re-render. Mutating objects in place, or plain fields, is the classic OnPush bug.

injectors.title: Services and injectors
injectors.description: A service lives as long as the injector that created it. Add and remove panels: each one provides its own TripMeter, shared with its child and destroyed with it, while the root FleetClock never changes.
injectors.routeScoped: Route providers create a third kind of injector, destroyed when you leave the route (withAutoCleanupInjectors).
injectors.routeLink: See it in the v21 demo
injectors.t1: Resolution starts at the component's element injector, walks up its ancestors and then the environment injectors (route → root). The first provider found wins.
injectors.t2: providedIn: 'root' or @Service() gives one tree-shakable singleton. providers: [] on a component gives one instance per component instance — ideal for state that belongs to a single widget.
injectors.t3: inject() works only in an injection context: field initializers, the constructor, factory functions or runInInjectionContext(). Anywhere else it throws NG0203.

rxjs.title: RxJS in practice
rxjs.intro: Signals now hold most component state, but events over time, cancellation and retries are still RxJS territory. Each demo runs the real operators; the tables beside them are what you would explain in a review.

flattening.title: switchMap vs mergeMap vs concatMap vs exhaustMap
flattening.description: Every click starts a fake request that takes 1.2 s. The same clicks go through all four operators at once, so you can compare what each one does with overlapping requests.
flattening.scenario: Play scenario (3 quick clicks, pause, 2 more)
flattening.finished: time window over — reset to try again

use.switchMap: search-as-you-type, route params: only the latest request matters.
use.mergeMap: independent work in parallel (uploads, deletes); pass a concurrency limit.
use.concatMap: writes that must keep their order (save, queue of commands).
use.exhaustMap: submit and login buttons: ignore clicks while a request is in flight.

flattening.t1: All four subscribe to an inner observable per value; they only differ in what happens when a new value arrives while an inner one is still running.
flattening.t2: switchMap cancels by unsubscribing — with HttpClient that aborts the HTTP request. Do not use it for writes: a cancelled POST may still have reached the server.
flattening.t3: mergeMap has no ordering guarantee; concatMap queues and can build up a backlog; exhaustMap drops values silently, so give the user feedback (disable the button).

subjects.title: Cold, hot and Subjects
subjects.description: Pick a source and subscribe A, B and C at different moments. Watch who receives what — and how often the producer runs.

cold.name: cold (defer)
cold.explain: Cold: the producer runs once per subscriber. Every subscribe is a new request — that is HttpClient's default.

shareReplay.name: shareReplay(1)
shareReplay.explain: Multicast and cached: the first subscriber triggers one execution, later subscribers get the cached last value.

subject.name: Subject
subject.explain: Hot, no memory: subscribers only get values emitted after they subscribed. Late subscribers miss everything before.

behavior.name: BehaviorSubject
behavior.explain: Hot with a current value: it needs an initial value and gives the latest one immediately on subscribe.

replay.name: ReplaySubject(2)
replay.explain: Hot with a buffer: late subscribers get the last two values replayed, then the live ones.

subjects.t1: Cold observables create their producer on subscribe (HTTP, timers, defer); hot ones share a producer that runs regardless of subscribers (DOM events, Subjects).
subjects.t2: Use shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true }) to share a request between consumers; without refCount the source stays subscribed after everyone leaves.
subjects.t3: Expose Subjects as asObservable() so consumers cannot call next(). For component state prefer a signal: same semantics as a BehaviorSubject, synchronous and glitch-free.

interop.title: Signals vs RxJS
interop.description: One click writes three values synchronously, both to a signal and to a Subject. See how each consumer observes the burst.
interop.explain: A Subject delivers every value immediately. A signal only holds the current value: effect() and toObservable() run once afterwards and see the last write. Signals model state; observables model events.

events.need: every occurrence of an event, cancellation

interop.t1: toSignal() subscribes immediately and unsubscribes with the injection context; give it an initialValue or handle undefined. It throws if the observable errors.
interop.t2: toObservable() emits asynchronously, once per change, with the latest value — intermediate synchronous writes are never seen.
interop.t3: Signals are glitch-free: consumers never see an inconsistent mix of old and new values. That makes them a poor fit for event streams where every value counts.

errors.title: Errors, retry and a stream that dies
errors.description: One click triggers the same failing server through three pipelines. The server fails twice, then recovers.
errors.server: Server: fails the first {{n}} calls in each column

log.dead: ✕ error reached subscribe(): stream closed, later clicks are ignored

errors.t1: An error terminates the observable it reaches. If it reaches the outer click stream, the feature is dead until the component is recreated.
errors.t2: Put catchError (and retry) inside the flattening operator, on the inner request, so only that request fails.
errors.t3: retry({ count, delay }) resubscribes to the source; with a cold HTTP observable that means a new request. Back off exponentially and only retry idempotent calls.

leaks.title: Subscription leaks
leaks.description: Both widgets subscribe to the same telemetry feed. Mount and unmount them a few times and watch the counters.
leaks.explain: Unmounting the leaky widget does not stop its subscription: the interval keeps running and keeps calling a destroyed component. The safe widget's subscription ends with its DestroyRef.
leaks.t1: Angular does not unsubscribe for you: subscriptions to long-lived sources (intervals, stores, router events, WebSockets) outlive the component unless something ends them.
leaks.t2: Prefer no manual subscription at all: toSignal() or the async pipe. When you must subscribe, use takeUntilDestroyed() in an injection context (or pass a DestroyRef).
leaks.t3: HttpClient requests complete after one response, so they rarely leak — but an unfinished one keeps its callback alive. Sources that never complete are the dangerous ones.

interview.title: Interview questions
interview.intro: Questions that come up in senior Angular interviews, each with a one-sentence answer to say out loud, the reasoning behind it and, where it helps, a live example in this app. Practice mode hides the answers until you have tried to answer yourself.
interview.practiceHint: Answers stay hidden until you reveal them, one by one.

signals.q: What is a signal, and how is it different from an Observable?
signals.short: A signal is a reactive value you can always read synchronously; an Observable is a stream of values over time that you subscribe to.
signals.long: A signal always has a current value, tracks who reads it and notifies only those consumers when it changes — no subscription, no teardown. Observables can emit zero, one or many values, can complete or error, and are lazy until subscribed. Signals model state; Observables model events and asynchronous work like debounced input, WebSockets or cancellable requests. Angular bridges both with toSignal() and toObservable().

computedEffect.q: computed() vs effect(): when do you use each?
computedEffect.short: computed() derives a value from other signals; effect() runs a side effect when signals change — use computed() whenever you can.
computedEffect.long: computed() is pure, lazy and memoized: it recalculates only when a dependency changed and someone reads it. effect() is for synchronising with the outside world — logging, localStorage, a chart library, analytics. Using an effect to set another signal is a smell: it causes an extra render and can create loops; that value should be a computed() or a linkedSignal(). Since v19, component effects run during change detection, after the inputs are set.

linkedSignal.short: It is a writable signal whose value resets from a source signal — derived state that the user can still override.
linkedSignal.long: Classic example: the selected city depends on the selected country, but the user can pick another city. computed() would not be writable, and an effect() copying the value would run one render too late. linkedSignal(() => cities(country())[0]) gives you the default, lets you set() it, and recomputes when the country changes. The long form receives the previous value, so you can keep the selection if it is still valid.

zoneless.q: How does change detection work without zone.js?
zoneless.short: Angular only schedules a check when something notifies it: a signal read by a template, a template event, an input change, markForCheck() or the async pipe.
zoneless.long: zone.js patched every async API and triggered a full app check after each callback. Zoneless Angular (stable in v20.2, default in v21) drops that: nothing happens unless a notification marks a view dirty. Signals are the finest notification — only the views that read them refresh, their ancestors are just traversed. The benefits are smaller bundles, no patched APIs, clearer stack traces and fewer useless checks; the cost is that mutating a plain field from a setTimeout or a third-party callback no longer updates the view.

onPush.q: What does OnPush do, and what changed in Angular 22?
onPush.short: OnPush skips a component unless it gets a new input reference, handles an event, reads a changed signal or is marked for check; in v22 it is the default.
onPush.long: Before v22 every component was checked whenever its parent was (Default) unless you opted into OnPush. Angular 22 flipped that: components are OnPush unless you write ChangeDetectionStrategy.Eager, the new name for Default. With signals this is natural, because signal reads notify precisely. What still breaks OnPush is in-place mutation: pushing into an array keeps the same reference, so neither the input check nor a signal sees a change.

lifecycleOrder.q: In which order do lifecycle hooks run?
lifecycleOrder.short: constructor, ngOnChanges, ngOnInit, ngDoCheck, ngAfterContentInit/Checked, ngAfterViewInit/Checked, then render hooks; ngOnDestroy at the end.
lifecycleOrder.long: ngOnChanges runs before ngOnInit and on every input change; ngOnInit runs once, when inputs are set. ngDoCheck and the two *Checked hooks run on every check of the parent — even when an OnPush child itself is skipped — so they must be cheap. Content hooks come before view hooks because projected content is resolved first. afterNextRender/afterRenderEffect run after the DOM is updated, and on destroy ngOnDestroy runs before DestroyRef callbacks. The live log in this app shows all of it.

afterRender.short: ngAfterViewInit fires when the view is created; afterNextRender runs once after the DOM is painted; afterRenderEffect re-runs after renders when its signals change.
afterRender.long: Use afterNextRender for one-time DOM work: focusing, measuring, initialising a third-party widget. afterRenderEffect is for keeping the DOM in sync with signals, split into earlyRead, write, mixedReadWrite and read phases so that Angular can batch reads and writes across components and avoid layout thrashing. Both are browser-only and never run on the server, which makes them SSR-safe. ngAfterViewInit is still fine for view queries, but viewChild() signals usually make it unnecessary.

diHierarchy.q: How does Angular resolve a dependency in the injector hierarchy?
diHierarchy.short: It walks up the element injectors of the component tree, then the environment injectors (route, then root); the first provider wins.
diHierarchy.long: providedIn: 'root' (or @Service() in v22) gives one tree-shakable singleton. providers on a component create one instance per component instance, shared by its children and destroyed with it — ideal for widget-level state. Route providers create an environment injector per route, destroyed on leave with withAutoCleanupInjectors(). Resolution modifiers like optional, self, skipSelf and host control where the search starts and stops.

injectionContext.q: What is an injection context, and why do you get NG0203?
injectionContext.short: inject() only works while Angular is creating something: field initializers, constructors, factory functions or runInInjectionContext(); elsewhere it throws NG0203.
injectionContext.long: inject() needs to know which injector to ask, and Angular only knows that during creation. In a click handler, a setTimeout or after an await the context is gone. Inject what you need in a field and use it later, or capture the Injector and call runInInjectionContext(). The same rule applies to functions built on inject(), such as takeUntilDestroyed() or toSignal(), unless you pass them an injector or DestroyRef explicitly.

standalone.q: Why standalone components, and what replaced NgModules?
standalone.short: Each component declares its own dependencies in imports, so the component is the unit of compilation, lazy loading and tree-shaking.
standalone.long: NgModules added an indirection: to know what a template could use you had to find the module that declared it. Standalone components (default since v19) import exactly what they use, routes lazy-load a component with loadComponent, and the app starts with bootstrapApplication() and provider functions like provideRouter() and provideHttpClient(). The result is less boilerplate, clearer dependencies and better tree-shaking.

signalInputs.q: input(), output() and model() vs @Input and @Output?
signalInputs.short: input() is a read-only signal, output() a lightweight event emitter and model() a two-way bindable signal — all type-safe and usable in computed().
signalInputs.long: Because input() is a signal, derived values are a computed() instead of ngOnChanges or setters, and input.required() is enforced at compile time. Transforms like numberAttribute replace manual parsing. output() no longer depends on RxJS's EventEmitter, and outputFromObservable() bridges streams. model() replaces the @Input/@Output pair for [(value)]. They also work with OnPush and zoneless without extra wiring.

controlFlow.q: Why is track mandatory in @for, and what changed from *ngFor?
controlFlow.short: track tells Angular how to recognise the same item between renders so it can move DOM nodes instead of recreating them.
controlFlow.long: @if, @for and @switch are built into the template compiler: no CommonModule import, better type narrowing and faster diffing. *ngFor had an optional trackBy and most code forgot it; @for makes track required, so you must think about identity. Track by a stable id; track by $index only for static lists. @empty handles the empty case without an extra @if.

deferBlocks.q: What does @defer do, and when would you use it?
deferBlocks.short: It moves a part of a template and its dependencies into a separate lazy chunk that loads on a trigger such as viewport, idle, interaction or timer.
deferBlocks.long: Use it for heavy widgets below the fold — charts, maps, editors — or content that only some users need. Triggers decide when the chunk is fetched; prefetch can download it earlier, for example on idle. @placeholder, @loading and @error cover the states, with minimum and after timings to avoid flicker. Only standalone dependencies used exclusively inside the block are split out; anything also imported elsewhere stays in the main bundle.

resourceApi.q: How do you load data with the Resource API?
resourceApi.short: resource()/httpResource() turn reactive params into an async value with status, error and reload, cancelling stale requests automatically.
resourceApi.long: httpResource(() => `/api/vehicles/${id()}`) refetches whenever id() changes and exposes value(), status(), error(), isLoading() and hasValue(). resource() does the same with any Promise-based loader and an AbortSignal; rxResource() takes an Observable stream. It replaces the toObservable + switchMap + toSignal pattern for reads. Watch out: value() throws in the error state, so check error() or hasValue() first. Mutations stay explicit calls.

signalForms.q: Reactive Forms vs Signal Forms: what is different?
signalForms.short: Signal Forms build the form from a signal model with a schema of validators; field state is signals, so there are no valueChanges subscriptions.
signalForms.long: In Reactive Forms the FormGroup owns the value and you sync it to your model; in Signal Forms form(model, schema) wraps your signal, and [formField] binds a control. Validation, disabled and hidden logic live in the schema and can be reactive. Submission handling maps server errors to fields. Signal Forms are stable in v22; Reactive Forms remain fully supported, and a large existing codebase does not need a rewrite.

routeParams.q: How do you read route parameters in a component?
routeParams.short: With withComponentInputBinding(), path params, query params and route data are bound to inputs with the same name.
routeParams.long: Instead of injecting ActivatedRoute and subscribing to paramMap, declare id = input.required<string>() and the router sets it, also when navigating between the same route with different params. Because it is a signal input, you can feed it straight into httpResource() or computed(). ActivatedRoute is still useful for fragments or when one component needs the whole snapshot.

flattening.q: switchMap, mergeMap, concatMap, exhaustMap: what is the difference?
flattening.short: They differ in what happens when a new value arrives while the previous inner observable is still running: switch cancels, merge runs in parallel, concat queues, exhaust ignores.
flattening.long: switchMap fits search-as-you-type and route changes, where only the latest result matters. mergeMap fits independent parallel work, ideally with a concurrency limit. concatMap fits writes that must keep their order. exhaustMap fits submit and login buttons, where repeated clicks should be ignored while a request is in flight. Picking one is a business decision about concurrency, and it should be visible in code review.

hotCold.q: What is the difference between a hot and a cold Observable?
hotCold.short: A cold Observable starts a new producer for each subscriber; a hot one shares a producer that runs independently of subscribers.
hotCold.long: HttpClient requests are cold: three subscribers mean three requests. DOM events and Subjects are hot: late subscribers miss what was emitted before. shareReplay({ bufferSize: 1, refCount: true }) turns a cold request into a shared, cached one; refCount: true unsubscribes from the source when the last subscriber leaves. Knowing which one you have explains duplicate requests and missing values.

subjects.q: Subject, BehaviorSubject or ReplaySubject: which one when?
subjects.short: Subject for pure events, BehaviorSubject for a current value with an initial state, ReplaySubject when late subscribers need the last n values.
subjects.long: A Subject has no memory. A BehaviorSubject requires an initial value and gives its current value on subscribe, which made it the classic state container. ReplaySubject(n) buffers the last n values. Expose them with asObservable() so only the owner can call next(). For component and service state today, a signal is simpler: same current-value semantics, synchronous reads, no subscriptions.

rxjsErrors.q: How do you handle errors in an RxJS stream without killing it?
rxjsErrors.short: Catch errors inside the flattening operator, on the inner request, so the outer stream survives; add retry with backoff for transient failures.
rxjsErrors.long: An error terminates the observable it reaches. A catchError at the end of clicks$.pipe(switchMap(...)) replaces the whole stream after the first error, and later clicks are silently ignored. Put retry({ count, delay }) and catchError on the inner observable instead. Use exponential backoff, only retry idempotent requests, and map errors into a typed state such as ProblemDetails for the UI.

unsubscribe.q: When and how do you unsubscribe?
unsubscribe.short: Avoid manual subscriptions with toSignal() or the async pipe; when you must subscribe, end it with takeUntilDestroyed().
unsubscribe.long: Sources that never complete — intervals, router events, stores, WebSockets — keep their subscription and callbacks alive after the component is destroyed. takeUntilDestroyed() ties the subscription to DestroyRef and works in services and directives too; outside an injection context, pass a DestroyRef. HttpClient requests complete after one response, so they rarely leak, but an unfinished request still holds its callback until it completes.

stillRxjs.q: With signals, do we still need RxJS?
stillRxjs.short: Yes, for events over time: debounce, cancellation, retries, WebSockets and combining async sources; signals handle state.
stillRxjs.long: Signals replaced BehaviorSubject-as-state and much of the async pipe. The Resource API covers most data loading, and debounced() in v22 covers simple debouncing. RxJS stays the right tool when every occurrence matters or time is part of the logic. The pragmatic rule: signals inside components and for state, RxJS at the edges for streams, with toSignal() and toObservable() as the boundary.

structure.q: How do you structure a large Angular application?
structure.short: By feature: lazy-loaded feature folders, a core for app-wide singletons and a shared UI library without business logic.
structure.long: Each feature owns its routes, components, services and state, and loads lazily, which keeps the initial bundle small and the boundaries clear. core holds interceptors, layout, i18n and models; shared/ui holds presentational components with inputs and outputs only. Path aliases and lint rules keep features from importing each other. In a monorepo the same idea scales with Nx libraries and enforced module boundaries.

stateManagement.q: Where should state live: signals, services or NgRx?
stateManagement.short: As close to where it is used as possible: local signals, then a component-scoped service, then an app-wide service; a store only when shared flows get complex.
stateManagement.long: UI state such as an open panel belongs in the component. State shared by a widget's children fits a service provided on that component. Session data or the cart fit a root service with signals and computed() selectors. NgRx — today often the Signal Store — pays off when many features share state, you need devtools and time travel, or many people must follow the same conventions. Server data is cached state, so the Resource API often removes the need for a store.

httpErrors.q: How do you handle HTTP errors across the application?
httpErrors.short: With functional interceptors that normalise errors into one typed shape, plus a UI state per request that shows them.
httpErrors.long: An error interceptor maps HttpErrorResponse to a typed model such as RFC 9457 ProblemDetails, so components never parse raw responses. Other interceptors add auth, retries for idempotent calls and a global loading indicator. Each screen still decides how to render loading, empty and error states — httpResource exposes them directly. Validation errors (422) are mapped onto form fields; unexpected ones go to logging.

testing.q: What is your testing strategy for an Angular app?
testing.short: Many fast component tests that use the DOM like a user, a few E2E tests for critical flows, and accessibility checks in CI.
testing.long: Component tests with Testing Library query by role and label, so they test behaviour and accessibility instead of implementation details. Services and pure functions get plain unit tests. Playwright covers the critical flows across browsers, and axe runs on every route. Coverage is a floor, not the goal. Tests must be deterministic: fake timers, a mock backend and no shared state.

accessibility.q: How do you make an Angular application accessible?
accessibility.short: Native HTML first, a proper accessible name for every control, keyboard support and focus management, verified with axe and keyboard tests.
accessibility.long: Use real buttons, links, labels and landmarks; add ARIA only when HTML has no equivalent. Composite widgets such as tabs, listboxes and menus come from Angular Aria or the CDK, which handle roles, focus and arrow keys. Announce async changes with live regions, move focus after navigation, respect prefers-reduced-motion and check contrast in both themes. Automated tools find about a third of the issues, so test with the keyboard and a screen reader too.

performance.q: An Angular app feels slow. How do you approach it?
performance.short: Measure first (Angular DevTools, Lighthouse, the bundle report), then fix the biggest cause: bundle size, unnecessary change detection or heavy rendering.
performance.long: Load time: lazy routes, @defer for heavy widgets, budgets in CI, image optimisation and caching headers. Runtime: OnPush and signals so fewer views are checked, track in @for, virtual scrolling for long lists, and moving heavy work out of templates into computed(). The DevTools profiler shows which components are checked and how long each takes. Always confirm with a measurement before and after.

bundle.q: How do you keep the bundle small?
bundle.short: Lazy-load routes and heavy widgets, keep dependencies tree-shakable, and enforce budgets in CI.
bundle.long: Lazy routes and @defer split code by need. injectAsync() (v22) loads a service only when it is first used, optionally prefetched on idle. Remove zone.js, avoid large libraries for small tasks, import specific entry points and check the build stats for duplicates. Budgets make the build warn or fail on regressions. Remember that shared code used by several lazy chunks may be hoisted into the initial bundle.

i18n.short: Runtime translation (e.g. ngx-translate) when users switch language live; build-time @angular/localize when performance matters most and a reload is fine.
i18n.long: @angular/localize compiles one build per locale: zero runtime cost, but switching language means loading another build. Runtime libraries load JSON files and switch instantly, at the cost of a small overhead and keys checked by tests rather than the compiler. Either way: update the lang attribute, format dates and numbers with the locale, plan for longer German text and right-to-left layouts, and test that every language has every key.

effectSync.q: Why shouldn't you use effect() to keep two signals in sync?
effectSync.short: Because it updates the second signal one step late, causes an extra render and can create loops; derive it with computed() or linkedSignal() instead.
effectSync.long: An effect runs after its dependencies change, so for a moment the two signals are inconsistent and the template may render the stale value first. Writing signals inside effects also makes the data flow hard to follow. If the value can be calculated, it is a computed(); if it must stay writable but reset when the source changes, it is a linkedSignal(). Keep effects for leaving the Angular world: storage, logging, imperative APIs.

mutation.q: An OnPush component does not update after items.push(newItem). Why?
mutation.short: push() mutates the array in place: the reference does not change, so neither the input check nor the signal notices.
mutation.long: OnPush compares input references, and signals compare values with Object.is by default. Mutating keeps the same object, so Angular sees no change and skips the view. Create a new array — items.update(list => [...list, newItem]) — or a new object for nested changes. Treating state as immutable is what makes OnPush and signals predictable; markForCheck() would only hide the problem.

switchMapSave.q: Why is switchMap a bad choice for a save button?
switchMapSave.short: switchMap cancels the previous request when a new click arrives, but the server may already have applied it — you lose the response, not the write.
switchMapSave.long: Unsubscribing aborts the HTTP request in the browser, which says nothing about the server: the first save may still be processed, out of order with the second. For writes use concatMap to keep the order, or exhaustMap to ignore clicks while a save is running — and disable the button so the user gets feedback. switchMap is for reads, where only the latest answer matters.

requiredInput.q: Why does reading a required input in a field initializer throw?
requiredInput.short: Field initializers run in the constructor, before Angular has set any input, so input.required() has no value yet (NG0950).
requiredInput.long: Inputs are set after the component is created and before ngOnInit. Reading this.amount() in a field initializer or the constructor therefore throws. Read it lazily instead: inside computed(), effect(), a template, or ngOnInit. Optional inputs return their default value early, which hides the same bug until the input becomes required.

thirdParty.q: In a zoneless app, a third-party library callback updates a field but the view does not change. How do you fix it?
thirdParty.short: Nothing notifies Angular, so store the value in a signal — or call markForCheck() if you cannot change the field.
thirdParty.long: With zone.js every callback triggered a full check, which hid this. Without zones, a plain field assignment in a map, chart or WebSocket callback schedules nothing. Setting a signal notifies exactly the views that read it. If the code is not yours, ChangeDetectorRef.markForCheck() marks the view and its ancestors for the next check. Events bound in the template already notify Angular.

trackIndex.q: What goes wrong if you use track $index on a list that can be reordered?
trackIndex.short: Angular reuses each DOM row and component by position, so after a reorder the rows keep their state but show other items.
trackIndex.long: With track $index, item 0 is always row 0. Sort or filter the list and Angular updates bindings instead of moving rows, so local component state — an expanded panel, an input's text, focus, an animation — stays in the wrong row. It is also slower, because more bindings change. Track by a stable identity such as the id or VIN; $index is only safe for static lists.

ng0100.short: In development mode Angular checks bindings twice; if a value changed between the two checks — usually set in a lifecycle hook during the same pass — it throws NG0100.
ng0100.long: It points to a one-directional data flow being broken: a child or a hook changes state its parent already rendered, for example in ngAfterViewInit. Wrapping the change in setTimeout only hides it. Fix the flow instead: derive the value with computed(), set it before the view is checked, or move one-time DOM-driven updates to afterNextRender() and write a signal, which schedules a new render. The error never appears in production builds, but the stale UI does.
